analysis.one_liner: Makes the repeal of the federal estate tax permanent.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in February 2005 and never received a vote, so the estate tax stayed in law.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2001 tax law phased out the federal estate tax, the tax on very large inheritances, but included a built-in expiration so the tax would come back in 2011. This bill would delete that expiration, making the repeal permanent so the estate tax would never return. It applies to a tax that only falls on estates worth several million dollars or more. The bill never left the Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates, since a tax of up to 45% on inheritances above several million dollars would disappear permanently. Under the 2001 law's schedule, the exemption had already risen to $2 million per person and the rate was falling; this bill would lock in full repeal after 2010.

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes the December 31, 2010 expiration in the 2001 tax law so that the repeal of the estate tax and the related generation-skipping transfer tax becomes permanent rather than returning automatically in 2011.
For heirs of the roughly one-in-a-hundred-plus estates large enough to owe the tax, this eliminates a tax of as much as 45% on what passes above the exemption amount.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. The estate tax is paid only on very large inheritances, so repeal does not raise anyone's taxes directly, but it removes revenue that would otherwise come from the wealthiest estates, leaving other taxes, borrowing, or program cuts to cover the difference.

drawbacks.text: Repealing a tax that falls almost entirely on multi-million-dollar inheritances forfeits tens of billions of dollars a year at full repeal, which must be made up through other taxes, more borrowing, or reduced government services.

Supporters argued the tax forces surviving spouses and heirs to sell family farms or small businesses to pay the bill; critics countered that the exemption levels already sheltered virtually all farms and most businesses, and that repeal functions as a large transfer to the wealthiest families.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: only heirs to the very largest estates ever owed this tax, and the 2001 law had already raised the exemption to $2 million per person and cut the rate. The cost is broad in a different way: permanent repeal removes a progressive revenue stream that could fund anything else, permanently. A family saving a farm faces no serious burden at these exemption levels, while a family inheriting $50 million saves tens of millions. The trade-off favors a small number of very wealthy households.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when this Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jon Kyl and seven other senators introduced the bill on February 17, 2005.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, where it received no markup, no vote, and no further action.
Twenty-four senators cosponsored the bill, 23 Republicans and one Democrat (Ben Nelson of Florida).
The bill died at the end of the 109th Congress in January 2007 without ever reaching the Senate floor, so the estate tax's scheduled return after 2010 remained in law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the estate tax remained on the books and the federal government kept a revenue source drawn almost entirely from multi-million-dollar estates. Wealthy heirs did not get the permanent repeal they sought, though the 2001 law's higher exemptions and lower rates already remained in effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal revenue and the estate tax

for.name: Jon Kyl
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the estate tax repeal permanent and led its Senate push.

for.name: Ben Nelson of Florida, Wayne Allard, George Allen, Conrad Burns, James Inhofe, Jim Talent, and John Thune
for.what_they_did: Joined Kyl in introducing the bill; Nelson (D-FL) was the only Democrat among them.

for.name: 23 of 24 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, keeping the repeal-permanency push alive in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (chaired by Chuck Grassley)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote, letting the bill sit without action until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Twenty-three of the bill's twenty-four cosponsors were Republicans; a single Democrat, Ben Nelson of Florida, crossed over, and no floor vote ever tested the full chamber.

industries.note: Permanent repeal of the estate tax would have saved multi-million-dollar families tens of millions per large estate. Because the tax is paid only by the largest estates and its loss must be made up by other taxpayers, its benefit runs against the public's fiscal interest.

industries.industry: Estate-planning lawyers, accountants, and life insurers
industries.note: A large industry of trust and estate professionals and insurance products built around sheltering estates from the tax would have lost much of its business under permanent repeal.
